messages.content:
You are FIXING a short WhatsApp quiz written for the children who sat in ONE real lesson. 1 of its 8 questions were rejected by our checks, and so was its lesson summary. You are writing ONE replacement for each rejected question, and a new "lesson_summary". Every other question is good and is staying exactly as it is — do not touch it, do not return it.

QUIZ LANGUAGE: English. Write EVERYTHING in English — every stem, option, explanation and feedback — even though the lesson was taught in Urdu: translate the teacher's own words and keep the lesson's own examples, numbers and names. An Urdu word may appear only when quoting a term the class used, in quotation marks.

REWRITE THESE QUESTIONS: q1

WHAT THESE CHILDREN WERE MEANT TO LEARN. A replacement stays on its own question's SLO, at its own question's level.
- S1 [taught at apply] Students will be able to compare unlike fractions using cross multiplication.
- S2 [taught at apply] Students will be able to compare unlike fractions using common denominators.
- S3 [taught at apply] Students will be able to order unlike fractions using cross multiplication.
- S4 [taught at apply] Students will be able to order unlike fractions using common denominators.

THE LESSON'S OWN MATERIAL — dress the replacement in it, so a child recognises the class in the quiz.
topic as the teacher named it: Comparing & ordering unlike fractions
the lesson's own examples: Comparing 2/3 of Hira's bottle with 3/5 of her friend's bottle.; Cross-multiplication: 2x5=10 (under 2/3) and 3x3=9 (under 3/5).; Comparison: 10 > 9, so 2/3 > 3/5.; Practice comparison of 3/4 and 2/5.; Practice ordering 2/9, 1/6, and 2/3.
the words used in class: unlike fractions, cross multiplication, common denominators, numerator, denominator, product

THE QUESTIONS THAT ARE STAYING. A replacement must not ask one of these again, and must not have the same answer as one of them.
  q0: When comparing fractions using cross multiplication, what do you multiply the numerator by?
  q2: You are comparing $\frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{2}{5}$ using cross multiplication. If you write $3 \times 5 = 15$ under $\frac{3}{4}$, what product should you write under $\frac{2}{5}$?
  q3: Look at the fraction bar. What fraction does the shaded part show?
  q4: To compare $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{3}{5}$ using common denominators, what is the smallest common denominator you can use?
  q5: When ordering fractions like $\frac{2}{9}$, $\frac{1}{6}$, and $\frac{2}{3}$ from greatest to smallest, which method is generally easier after finding the cross products?
  q6: Look at the number line. Which point is at $\frac{1}{2}$?
  q7: To order $\frac{2}{9}$, $\frac{1}{6}$, and $\frac{2}{3}$ using common denominators, what is the smallest common denominator for all three fractions?

EVERY QUESTION TESTS SOMETHING NO OTHER QUESTION TESTS. No two questions in the quiz may have the same correct answer on the same fact: the same question with its options in another order, with other wrong options, or with a few words added or changed is the SAME question, and a child would answer it twice. A question shape may be used again only with different numbers or a different item from the lesson (round 18, then round 16; the article before "kite", then before "tree"), so that its correct answer is different too. Before you return, read the questions side by side: where two test the same thing, write a question on something else in place of the later one, keeping the number of questions as it is.

REJECTED — write one new question for each, except a question marked REPAIR IN PLACE: return that one as it stands, with only the words its complaints name changed.

  the question being thrown away: "Hira had $\frac{2}{3}$ of a bottle and her friend had $\frac{3}{5}$ of a bottle. To compare them using cross multiplication, what is the first product you would calculate for Hira's bottle?"
  its options were: $2 \times 5$ | $2 \times 3$ | $3 \times 5$
